Au cours de la fin de semaine qui a suiv: During the weekend after October 11, I was browsing Asian forums and saw that many people were angry about a segment aired on the Canadian entrepreneurship show Dragon’s Den. The reason for the fury? Two white Quebec entrepreneurs appeared on the show and pitched their bubble tea company, Bobba. Simu Liu, a Chinese-Canadian investor on the show’s panel, questioned them about their approach and raised some concerns about cultural appropriation. Since then, Asian communities around the world have been standing behind him and are angry at the company.
Comme je suis moi-même Asiatique et que: As an Asian person living in Quebec myself, this affair caught my attention. I followed it as it unfolded on social media, and I noticed that Winston Chan and David Trang, francophone Asian Quebecers, made statements about the situation that circulated widely in the Asian community in Quebec. Many people are relieved to finally see voices rising on this issue, and are fed up with not being heard when they denounce cases of cultural appropriation.
Mais pourquoi autant de personnes sont-e: But why are so many people this furious, and why do they feel they aren’t being taken seriously? As a journalist, I wanted to dig into the question to better understand the nuances of the cultural appropriation Asians experience in Quebec. I wanted to explore the issue from several angles, so I spoke with the owners of a Montréal bubble tea café, a food specialist, a television producer and an entrepreneur. Their views bring out several perspectives on this type of cultural appropriation.
Il a été très difficile durant la rédact: While working on this report, it was very difficult to find a bubble tea shop willing to answer my questions. First, I wanted to speak with a representative of a local business run by Asians, which immediately ruled out the many multinational bubble tea chains in Montréal. Second, the employees of these businesses are very busy running their shops. So I struggled to pin down an interview time, and I was turned down many times.
J’aurais aimé discuter avec les entrepre: I would have liked to speak with the Bobba entrepreneurs to get their opinion on this issue and open a dialogue but, unfortunately, it was impossible to reach them.
J’espère que j’ai rendu justice à cette: I hope I have done justice to this complex issue and represented all of its nuances well.
Un segment télévisé sur le thé aux perle: A television segment on bubble tea has touched a nerve in the Asian diaspora. The drink – made of tea, milk and tapioca pearls – originated in Taiwan and is also known as “bubble tea” or “boba.” It is an important cultural symbol, a connection to the roots of Taiwanese and, more broadly, Asian culture.
<strong>Le 10 octobre dernier, Sébastien: Last October 10, Sébastien Fiset and Jessica Frenette, two white francophone Quebec entrepreneurs, appeared on Dragon’s Den to pitch their bubble tea company, Bobba, to a panel of potential investors. Their venture drew mixed reactions: some saw it as cultural appropriation of the Asian roots of bubble tea, others as an opportunity to popularize the drink even more. Report.
Lors de leur passage à l’émission, Sébas: During their appearance on the show, Sébastien Fiset and Jessica Frenette claim to be revolutionizing bubble tea. “You’ve surely heard of bubble tea, that trendy sweet drink people line up for and whose contents you’re never sure about,” Jessica Frenette says right off the bat on television. “Those days are over with Bobba!” Sébastien Fiset exclaims. The duo explains that they make the drink “healthier” by using fruit juice and offering it in bottle format. They say they are innovating by creating popping pearls and adding alcohol inside them. The entrepreneurs say they launched the project because it was trendy and there was a lot of money to be made.
En face, Simu Liu, un Sino-Canadien drag: Across from them, Simu Liu, a Chinese-Canadian Dragon on the show, looks confused. “There’s a cultural appropriation problem. The problem is taking something very distinctly Asian in its identity and supposedly improving it; that’s something I have a problem with,” the investor says. Sébastien Fiset then answers that Bobba “is no longer an ethnic product, not with the popping pearls, we took the Asian version and made it with fruits and juices,” he says. Asked by the panel about the product’s Asian origins, Sébastien Fiset mentions a Taiwanese supplier. The company ultimately accepts Manjit Minhas’s investment offer – <l1>an offer she has since withdrawn</l1>.
Depuis la diffusion de l’émission, <l1>l: Since the episode aired, the Asian diaspora has been denouncing this Quebec company’s cultural confiscation. The controversy grew so large that Simu Liu spoke out on social media. He said that, while he appreciated the discussion on cultural appropriation the segment generated, it was unacceptable for internet users to send death threats to Sébastien Fiset and Jessica Frenette – a position shared by Dragon’s Den. Two days after the broadcast, the investor agreed to invest in TWRL, a bubble tea company founded by two women from Taiwan and Hong Kong, after having publicly supported Simu Liu. Bobba has since posted an apology on its Instagram account.
Lorsqu’on entre dans le café de thé aux: Walking into the Ocha bubble tea café in Montréal, you are immediately won over by the airy decor and the two giant eggshell chairs to the left of the door. Young people sitting on stools wait for their orders or chat with friends. Kevin Tulud, one of the café’s owners and founders, bustles behind the counter, concocting drinks from ingredients his team has carefully selected. The noise of the drink-making machines sets the mood in the room.
Fondé en 2022 par Kevin Tulud et Jonah X: Founded in 2022 by Kevin Tulud and Jonah Xu, two second-generation Asians in their thirties, the Ocha bubble tea shop offers flavours and colours on its menu that are still rare in Montréal, such as ube lattes and mochi donuts. Ocha is one of a dozen or so bubble tea shops opened by Asians over the past 15 years near the Guy-Concordia metro station, in a neighbourhood with a large Asian population.
Jonah Xu, d’origine chinoise et hongkong: Jonah Xu, of Chinese and Hong Kong descent, and Kevin Tulud, of Filipino descent, look back on their teenage memories: their friends used bubble tea as a tool for community gathering. “We grew up in Montréal, and the Asian community was small, especially back then. But what drew us in?” says Jonah Xu nostalgically. “Back then there was karaoke, Chinese school, but also the chilling spot, as we say. We’d go to L2 [a bubble tea café in Chinatown, ED.], for example, […] and we’d chill there.” His business partner agrees: “For me, bubble tea is about relaxing with friends, while enjoying excellent drinks and maybe some good food too. It’s just being together,” he says with a big smile.
Désireux d’offrir aux autres les belles: Wanting to give others the great experiences of their teenage years, the two entrepreneurs created Ocha. They have worked into their drinks and snacks Asian products that are still rarely seen in Montréal. “Actually, we try as much as possible to use products that other shops don’t have,” explains Jonah Xu. To do so, the two entrepreneurs travel to Asia to select ingredients. They also work with partners from ethnic communities across Asia to create a pan-Asian menu. “For example, the Viet matcha coffee. It’s a combination of Japanese matcha and Vietnamese coffee. Or the ube latte, which is Filipino, just to name a few,” Jonah Xu says. “Our goal is really to find as many products as we can that we love, that are popular, and bring them to Montréal.”
<strong>« Comment veux-tu vendre quelque: “How can you sell something you don’t really know?”
Kevin Tulud et Jonah Xu soulignent qu’il: Kevin Tulud and Jonah Xu stress that it is essential to respect the origins and traditions associated with bubble tea. “What really irked me was that they say it’s healthier,” Jonah Xu says. Contrary to the Bobba entrepreneurs’ claims, popping pearls are found in many bubble tea shops in Montréal. The owner of Ocha points out that this product is even sold mainly in North America. In his view, including these pearls, which are high in sugar, runs counter to Bobba’s health-focused marketing message.
« Puis, ils affirment que, dans les [aut: “Then they claim that in [other] bubble tea products, you don’t really know what’s in them,” Jonah Xu says indignantly. “That shocked me a bit, because in reality, most Asians know what products are used in bubble teas!”
Lors de son <em>pitch</em>, Sébastien Fi: During his pitch, Sébastien Fiset mentioned that he had gotten into this venture because he saw the chance to make a big profit and that Bobba was no longer an “ethnic product.” Kevin Tulud finds this disheartening. “If they truly believe that bottled bubble tea is trendy right now and that they can easily make money, I’m sorry, but that’s not the right approach,” he says. “Imagine the research, the development, the testing. All of that is hours and hours of work before launching a flavour. It’s not quick money, it’s hard to make money! I think Bobba had no passion for its product, and that’s what sparked the controversy.”
Il est possible pour un entrepreneur de: For his part, Jonah Xu believes it is possible for an entrepreneur to start a business with a product that comes from a culture other than their own, as long as they do it respectfully. He cites, for example, non-Japanese chefs who train in Japan to learn sushi-making traditions before opening a sushi business.
« Si les entrepreneurs de [Bobba] avaien: “If the [Bobba] entrepreneurs had done their research, had made their pitch differently, with better facts, most Quebec Asians or Asians around the world would have been fine with their products,” he believes. “Because canned bubble tea exists. In fact, you can buy it here, everywhere, it already exists. It’s just a question of how [Bobba] goes about it.” “How can you sell something you don’t really know?” adds Kevin Tulud. According to the Ocha co-founder, the Bobba entrepreneurs should have been better prepared to face Simu Liu, an Asian investor with cultural expertise in bubble tea. Still, Kevin Tulud doesn’t want to fuel the controversy against the company. He would prefer that a dialogue begin with Bobba’s owners to educate them and steer them in the right direction.

Rachel Cheng, une spécialiste en aliment: Rachel Cheng, a food specialist who has worked in the community sector for more than 10 years, was disappointed, but not surprised, by Bobba’s pitch on Dragon’s Den. “In Quebec, we kind of get used to this, to this kind of talk,” she says. “There’s a cultural appropriation problem because we tend to ignore these kinds of issues, especially in the food sector.” Having grown up in Toronto but settled in Quebec for more than 16 years, Rachel Cheng says she felt culturally alienated after moving. She frowns as she recalls that period, as though painful memories are resurfacing. “There are a lot of important conversations happening in English elsewhere in the world about cultural appropriation, around equity, anti-racism, which I think […] don’t always break through into the francophone world because of language,” she says.
Dans le cadre de son travail avec des or: In her work with community organizations engaged in fair production and access to culturally appropriate food, she sees that questions of cultural appropriation are often poorly understood. “I see so many examples in food, where recipes from other cultures are used. While it may be done with good intentions, there’s often a lack of effort to develop real cultural interest or curiosity in order to respect those traditions,” explains Ms.<sup></sup> Cheng. She often suggests that the organizations she works with be aware of the power dynamics present in society. “If you’re a [white] francophone Quebec chef, that gives you certain levels of privilege, and also a responsibility somewhere to name the other cultures [that] you [use to make a profit].”
« Le thé aux perles, c’est quelque chose: “Bubble tea has existed since the 1980s in Taiwan. At its base, it’s three super simple ingredients: black tea, a bit of milk and tapioca pearls,” the specialist points out. According to her, many Asian cultures have long culinary traditions devoted to teas. There are traditions, like that of traditional Chinese medicine, where the best herbs and plants are chosen to prepare a tea that heals body and mind. There are others that are more ceremonial – like the tea ceremonies held at Chinese weddings – or spiritual – like the matcha tea ceremonies linked to Zen Buddhism. “So when someone who isn’t from an Asian culture, and doesn’t know the culinary tradition with tea, says their tea is better for your health, and that it’s new, it touches on several very sensitive points of Taiwanese identity, of Asian identity,” explains Ms.<sup></sup> Cheng.
La vive réaction de la communauté asiati: The Asian community’s strong reaction is partly tied to the history of the Chinese restaurant in the 1960s, which stigmatized Asian cuisine, adds the food specialist. “[This syndrome] appeared in a medical journal. A doctor said: ‘When I eat at a Chinese restaurant, I don’t feel well afterwards.’ Then, over the years, many people [agreed with him and] blamed monosodium glutamate (MSG),” she recounts. “Like anything, like salt or sugar, it should be consumed in moderation, of course. But since then, [this syndrome] has been refuted in other scientific articles.” That is why, she explains, Bobba’s assertion that with bubble teas “you’re never sure about the contents” reopened old wounds in the Asian community. It triggered immense anger toward the company. “For them to say they made their tea cleaner, more clean, healthier – it’s factually false and it’s just a bit ignorant,” she says.
Lorsque le producteur numérique David Tr: When digital producer David Trang saw Bobba’s Dragon’s Den segment go by on TikTok, he was shocked. After a weekend spent analyzing internet users’ reactions, he realized the outcry was growing and spoke out on Instagram. As a child, he suffered the consequences of the historical distrust Asian cuisine has endured: “When I was young and drank bubble tea, I was judged, ridiculed and bullied because I was drinking something that seemed weird, gross and unusual,” he says. “Today, it’s the same kind of people who want to appropriate this recipe and its whole history.”
Pour le producteur, la réaction des autr: For the producer, the reaction of the other panellists to Simu Liu’s concerns is linked to the racial dynamics Asians experience, as they are often perceived as model minorities. He sees “real gaslighting” in it. In this context, it’s hard to be taken seriously when you dare to denounce anything, he says. Rachel Cheng shares this analysis. “We tend not to be listened to when we make demands.”
« Voir les autres dragons ignorer son op: “Seeing the other Dragons ignore his opinion, ridicule him on television was triggering for me, because it’s always the same story when a situation like this involves Asians,” confides David Trang. Bobba’s pitch on Dragon’s Den troubled him. “But at the same time, I’m glad it aired because [otherwise] we wouldn’t be having this discussion today. Did they do it so it would blow up and go viral? It could be an editorial decision. If so, other questions arise: is it ethical to profit from something like this, to make it go viral and get people reacting?” he wonders.
Pour David Trang, cette controverse renv: For David Trang, this controversy points to a deeper problem, tied to the way Asian culture is colonized and appropriated, not to mention the systemic racism that goes unrecognized in Quebec.
Winston Chan, qui œuvre en entrepreneuri: Winston Chan, who has worked in entrepreneurship for more than 10 years, says he was proud to see Simu Liu on television, an entrepreneur in a position of power. Despite his busy schedule, he wanted to speak with us. “It’s very rare to see Asians in Canada or in North America in a position of authority. I think it bothered a lot of people,” he says.
Selon lui, se lancer en affaires avec un: In his view, starting a business with a product from another culture is possible if it’s done with respect for its origins. “Cultural appreciation is when you get involved with people from those communities in the design, marketing, promotion and communication of the product,” he lists. The Cambodian restaurant Pumpui, the Indian snack bar Super Qualité and the Japanese restaurant Fleurs et Cadeaux are, in his eyes, examples of Asian cultural appreciation in Montréal. “If we take the case of Bobba, there’s no Asian reference whatsoever. That was in fact the entrepreneurs’ intention; they even said it was no longer an ethnic product.”
M. Chan critique aussi vivement l’absenc: Mr. Chan also sharply criticizes the absence of any mention of the Taiwanese supplier in the company’s communications and on the product’s packaging. In his view, Bobba should have tried to understand the Asian community’s relationship with bubble tea. “It’s a pretext for people to gather with friends in communities all over the world. For them, it’s a link to Asia. It represents much more than a drink,” he explains.
De son côté, Rachel Cheng aimerait invit: For her part, Rachel Cheng would like to invite the Bobba entrepreneurs to try a quality bubble tea. “I want to invite them to have a real bubble tea, a really good tea […] to let them taste the diversity of flavours and see the role bubble tea plays in Asian communities,” she continues. “They’ve already taken a trip to Taiwan, they work with someone there who makes recipes. I’d say they need to do that, but [push] even [further] and see why their packaging, their story, their product is so hurtful to the Asian community. They need a moment of introspection.”
Après avoir essayé plusieurs fois de com: After trying several times to reach Bobba by email and on social media, La Converse received no response. The company’s representatives stated on Instagram that they “were deeply sorry to have hurt [Asian communities] by [their] words and [their] actions during the show.” It was not their “intention to cause harm and show disrespect to the community that created and popularized this beloved drink.” They also say they “take full responsibility for the impact of [their] actions” and state that they want to “commit to learning more about the impacts of cultural appropriation.”
